title: perf-regression-alert-triage-workflow
content:
Purpose
This is a working runbook for handling performance regressions detected by our monitoring: how to validate alerts, run quick triage, bisect potential causes (code, model, infra), and perform canary comparisons. Intended audience: eng-serving-runtime on-call and SREs.

Scope
- Latency spikes (p50/p95/p99)
- Throughput drops / tail latency regressions
- Token/sec or GPU utilization anomalies
- Memory growth / OOM related to inference kernels or batching
- Changes after releases (runtime, model weights, CUDA/mkl, container images)

High-level flow
1) Alert intake: confirm signal and scope
2) Quick blast (5-15m): reproduce or collect minimal evidence
3) Triage: is this canary/rollback candidate?
4) Bisect: narrow to PRs, model change, infra change, or workload shift
5) Remediate: rollback, revert, patch; or tune config (batching/quantization)
6) Postmortem: link to incident, metrics before/after, root cause, next actions

1) Alert intake (on-call)
- Primary dashboards: Perf Regression Overview (Grafana), Per-route latency, GPU pool metrics. Link: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/serving/perf-regressions
- Check alert details: which metric (p95/p99), threshold breached, time window, affected routes/models.
- Scope: single customer? single region? all traffic? dedicated pools only?
- Immediate actions (first 10 minutes):
  - Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty/Slack
  - Post initial note in #serving-runtime with alert link, top-3 suspicion (recent deploy? config change? load spike?), and a pointer to the Grafana panel.

2) Quick evidence collection (5-15m)
- Grab these graphs and snapshots:
  - p50/p95/p99 across last 6h vs 24h (route-level)
  - Token/sec and request/sec curves
  - GPU util / memory / SM stalls / encoder/decoder breakdown if available
  - Host/container-level CPU steal and network IO
  - Recent deploys: query CD pipeline and GitHub to see image tags deployed in the last 6h.
- Run a quick synthetic query against a representative route/model from a benign client and measure latency (curl or client SDK with timing). Example: 
  - curl -s -w "time_total:%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate?model=redwood-####" -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
- Check canary pool (if we have a dedicated canary) and compare same synthetic query result/latency.

3) Triage decision trees
- If only one customer or one region affected -> likely config/traffic/regression localized. Contact CS/Customer.
- If multiple routes/models in same pool -> likely runtime/infra or kernel regression. Check for recent PRs to serving-runtime or new runtime images.
- If only one model shows p99 growth but others okay -> suspect model weights, tokenizer changes, or prompt length distribution.
- If GPU memory pressure increases -> suspect new kv-cache behavior, batching changes, or changed sequence lengths.

4) Bisect process (code/model/infra)
- Quick checklist to narrow candidate class:
  - Check deploy history (CI/CD events): timestamp of last deploy per cluster.
  - Check package versions on hosts (cuda, cuDNN, Triton/runtime dependencies) using config mgmt or node exporter metadata.
  - Query logs for errors/exceptions around time window.
  - Compare canary vs main: if canary running older image and healthy -> suspect recent deploy.

- Bisect by PR: (when suspect code change)
  1. Identify PRs merged in the 6-48h window that touch serving-runtime, scheduler, batching, or kernel wrappers. Use GitHub search/CI links.
  2. If < 5 candidates, run local/regression CI with a small perf harness (see ./tools/perf-harness) to reproduce p95/p99 differences.
  3. If > 5 candidates, use binary search on deploy snapshots: rollback canary to previous image and compare.

- Bisect by model: (when suspect model change)
  1. Verify model version pinning and rollout history (console/rollouts).
  2. Re-run synthetic requests against previous model version in a staging/dedicated test pool.
  3. Observe KV cache usage and tokenization differences.

- Bisect by infra: (when suspect infra/drivers)
  1. Check recent kernel/driver updates, node reboots, or autoscaler events.
  2. Inspect host-level metrics: GPU driver errors, dmesg OOM/killed tasks.
  3. If suspected, move a subset of traffic to a node with older driver or spin up new nodes with previous AMI to compare.

5) Canary comparisons (how we run them)
- Canary types: passive (sampling), active (test traffic), and shadow (mirror). Use the canary that matches the behavior.
- Steps for active canary comparison:
  1. Spin up canary pool pinned to previous image/model/config.
  2. Run identical workload (synthetic) to both pools for minimum 5k tokens or 5 minutes to capture tail behavior.
  3. Collect p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU metrics, batching distribution, and KV cache hit rate.
  4. Run A/B statistical test (Mann-Whitney U for latency distributions, or bootstrap of p95) and record p-values and effect sizes.
  5. If p99 difference > 10-20% or statistically significant with practical effect, consider rollback.

6) Quick mitigations (low-risk)
- Toggle autoscaling/burst to limit cold starts if cold-start spikes identified.
- Temporarily reduce batch size or disable dynamic batching (if batching regression suspected) to reduce tail latency.
- Fallback to a known-good model variant (lower-latency quantized variant) for critical routes.

7) Rollback / Revert guidance
- If canary shows regression and quick mitigations insufficient, open a revert PR for the last deploy and coordinate with CD to roll back.
- For infra/driver rollbacks, follow SRE host rollback playbook (link in linked_artifacts).

8) Postmortem and follow-ups
- Required for any rollback or outage > 30 minutes. Include: timeline, root cause hypothesis, evidence (graphs, canary runs, bisect steps), revert PRs, and next actions (tests, monitoring, config guards). Link PMs and CS for customer impact.
- Add automated sanity checks to CI if code change was root cause: e.g., micro-benchmarks for kernel call latencies, p95 harnesses for critical routes.

Useful queries and commands
- Grafana: export panel JSON and attach to incident.
- Logs: 
  - kubectl logs -n serving -l app=worker --since=1h | grep -i "warning\|error\|latency"
- Perf harness: ./tools/perf-harness/run.sh --model redwood-#### --duration 300 --concurrency 4 --capture-latency > /tmp/run.json
- GPU metrics collector: /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-metrics --since 3600 --output /tmp/gpu.json

Diagnostic artifacts to attach to ticket
- Time-series snapshots (p50/p95/p99) per route and aggregated
- Batching histogram (requests per batch) and batch size distribution over window
- GPU memory & utilization per host
- Synthetic request logs and raw latencies for canary runs
- Reproducer (perf-harness config) used to trigger regression locally

Common gotchas / past incidents
- Changing default batching timeout by 5-10ms had outsized p99 impact on low-latency routes (SERV-2011).
- Quantization knob mis-applied caused one kernel path to use slower fallback (root cause: dtype mismatch in model loader).
- Tokenization change (newline handling) increased average sequence length and indirectly raised p99.

Appendix: quick checklist for on-call (copyable)
- Acknowledge alert and paste link in #serving-runtime.
- Snapshot Grafana panels and note affected routes/models.
- Run quick synthetic against main and canary.
- Check recent deploys and commit history for serving-runtime and model rollouts.
- If regression confirmed and canary shows difference, start revert and notify stakeholders.
- Attach artifacts to Jira ticket and create postmortem if needed.

Notes / TODOs
- Add an automated CI micro-benchmark job to run on serving-runtime PRs that exercises the hot path batching/kernel code.
- Add a templated Grafana report for quick export in incidents.
- Add a small library to produce reproducible synthetic workloads from the console.

Authors and contact
- Maintainer: Samir Gupta (samir@redwood.ai)
- Contributors: Asha Patel, Claire Nguyen, Miguel Torres

Last tested: synthetic canary comparison workflow tested on 2026-01-18 with image rollback scenario (notes in linked GitHub PR).
